title: Strategic Leadership
description: Editable version of the complete Mayne Leadership Strategic Leadership course, including its original explanations, practice activities, application, and reflection prompts.
author: Joshua Mayne

blocks.title: Lead beyond your line of sight.

blocks.body: Strategic thinking determines what matters. Strategic leadership mobilizes people around it.
Shape direction. Align systems. Build leaders. Influence beyond authority. Communicate through complexity. Protect trust while achieving results.
Approx. 2 hours · Interactive self-paced course · Progress saved on this device

blocks.title: From personal control to organizational alignment.

blocks.body: Strategic leadership is not a bigger version of direct supervision. As scope expands, leaders increasingly work through vision, priorities, systems, subordinate leaders, relationships, resources, communication, and trust.
What you will practice

Lead at scale
Understand how leadership changes from foundation to direct, organizational, and strategic levels.

Use six meta-competencies
Mental agility, vision, decision shaping, team building, communication, and ethical ambition.

Move from hero to architect
Create conditions that allow others to make aligned decisions without waiting for you.

Influence without control
Lead down, up, across, and out when responsibility exceeds formal authority.

Create strategic alignment
Make intent, priorities, stakeholders, risk, learning rhythm, and leader action visible.

blocks.title: See More → Think Deeper → Look Further → Lead Broader

blocks.body: Strategic Thinking improves the quality of understanding. Strategic Leadership asks what you do with that understanding when other people, systems, and organizations must move with you.
The work shifts from solving tasks to creating clarity, alignment, trust, and systems that preserve intent.

blocks.title: Your method of influence changes as the system grows.

blocks.body: Personal control → Alignment
You cannot personally direct every decision. You create intent, boundaries, priorities, and relationships so others can move together.
Tasks → Conditions
The strategic leader increasingly shapes systems, resources, structures, decision rights, incentives, and communication rhythms.
Individual execution → Leader network
Success depends on second-level leaders and partners who understand enough intent to act well when you are absent.
What works with a small team can fail at scale: personally solving every issue, relying on informal communication, or assuming intent is understood because it was said once.
Open all four. The same character matters at every level; the application changes.

items.title: FOUNDATION
items.text: Character · competence · trust — Self-awareness, ethics, credibility, competence, and trust support every other level.

items.title: DIRECT
items.text: Teams + individuals — Influence is immediate and personal; leaders can often see the work and interact directly.

items.title: ORGANIZATIONAL
items.text: Systems + organizations — Influence travels through processes, resources, subordinate leaders, structures, and competing priorities.

items.title: STRATEGIC
items.text: Enterprise + environment — Direction, external relationships, long-term conditions, resource tradeoffs, and indirect influence dominate.

blocks.title: The job moves from doing the work to creating the conditions for the work.

blocks.body: Personal influence→Indirect influence
Immediate outcomes→Long-term conditions
Control→Alignment
Answers→Better questions
Work→Systems
Personal expertise→Integrated expertise
Which transition is hardest for strong performers?

blocks.title: Your most difficult leadership transition
blocks.body:
Select the transition you find most difficult.

  • Personal → indirect influence
  • Immediate → long-term
  • Control → alignment
  • Answers → better questions
  • Work → systems
  • Expertise → integration

blocks.title: Why is this transition difficult—and what behavior would help?
blocks.body: Why is this transition difficult—and what behavior would help?

A strength at one level can become a liability at another. Decisiveness can become premature closure; expertise can become over-control; responsiveness can keep the leader permanently on the dance floor.

blocks.title: Strategic scope increases the cost of weak foundations.

blocks.body: Character
Values, ethics, discipline, accountability, consistency, and the willingness to place mission and stewardship above ego.
Presence
Credibility, resilience, calm under scrutiny, confidence without arrogance, and consistency across audiences.
Intellect
Judgment, innovation, mental agility, systems understanding, and the ability to integrate expert advice.
Competencies still come down to leading, developing, and achieving—but the scale, time horizon, and indirect nature of influence change dramatically.

blocks.title: Strategic leadership is visible in the current Executive Core Qualifications.

blocks.body: For federal leaders, OPM's current ECQs connect rule of law, efficiency, merit and competence, leading people, and achieving results. Strategic thinking is explicitly included under Achieving Results.

items.title: Rule of Law + Founding Principles
items.text: Uphold constitutional government, rule of law, and service to the American people.

items.title: Driving Efficiency
items.text: Strategically manage resources, budget, process, and technology to improve efficiency.

items.title: Merit + Competence
items.text: Demonstrate technical competence, problem solving, agility, resilience, and exceptional-quality work.

items.title: Leading People
items.text: Inspire people toward mission and goals while building a high-performance, high-accountability culture.

items.title: Achieving Results
items.text: Translate strategy into action, innovate, think strategically, and align results to organizational goals.

blocks.body: The leadership challenge is not simply to move faster. It is to achieve legitimate, effective, accountable outcomes while managing people, resources, technology, risk, and long-term organizational interests.

blocks.title: Six behaviors help leaders operate at enterprise scale.

blocks.body: Open all six. The framework is adapted from strategic-leadership research and translated into practical leader behavior.

items.title: Mental Agility
items.text: Move between details, systems, and future implications; hold competing truths long enough to understand them.

items.title: Vision
items.text: Describe a desired future condition and make intent clear enough to guide decisions when you are absent.

items.title: Decision Shaping
items.text: Clarify decision ownership, frame options, surface tradeoffs, and improve the quality of the decision environment.

items.title: Team Building
items.text: Build trust, clarity, roles, rhythm, and psychological safety across functions and boundaries.

items.title: Communication
items.text: Translate complexity through layers and audiences without hiding risk or changing the core truth.

items.title: Ethical Ambition
items.text: Achieve meaningful results with integrity, stewardship, accountability, and long-term legitimacy.

blocks.body: Strategic leaders move between details, systems, and future implications. They can hold competing truths long enough to understand them before locking onto an answer.

blocks.title: THE DETAIL
blocks.body: What immediate issue is pulling attention?

blocks.title: THE SYSTEM
blocks.body: What larger process, pattern, or dependency surrounds it?

blocks.title: THE FUTURE
blocks.body: What future implication or second-order effect matters?

blocks.title: THE BETTER QUESTION
blocks.body: What question helps you regain altitude?
Mental agility is not knowing everything. It is integrating expertise without becoming trapped in one frame.
A strategic vision is not a slogan. It describes a desired future condition clearly enough to guide decisions when the leader is absent.

Weak: “We need to improve communication.”
Stronger: Describe the future condition, why it matters, and what decisions it should guide.

blocks.title: DESIRED FUTURE CONDITION
blocks.body: What should be true when this is working well?

blocks.title: WHY IT MATTERS
blocks.body: How does this connect to mission, people, customers, or public value?

blocks.title: DECISION GUIDANCE
blocks.body: What should leaders be able to decide without asking you?

blocks.title: ONE-SENTENCE INTENT
blocks.body: We are creating ___ so that ___.
The test of vision is not whether it sounds inspiring. The test is whether people can use it to make aligned decisions when you are not in the room.

blocks.title: Sometimes you decide. Sometimes you shape the decision environment.

blocks.body: Strategic leaders clarify decision rights, frame choices, surface tradeoffs, and make the type of request explicit.

blocks.title: ENDS
blocks.body: Desired condition

blocks.title: WAYS
blocks.body: Broad approach

blocks.body: People, resources, authorities, time

blocks.title: What are you asking leadership for?
blocks.body:
Choose the type of request you are preparing.

  • Recommendation
  • Decision
  • Request for guidance
  • Request for concurrence
Use explicit language: is this a recommendation, a decision, a request for guidance, or a request for concurrence? Unclear decision rights create delay and shadow decision-making.

blocks.title: Strategic teams often include experts you do not command.

blocks.body: Select the conditions your cross-functional team most needs to strengthen, then design the operating environment around them.

blocks.title: Two strategic-team conditions
blocks.body:
Identify at least two conditions that most need attention.

  • Trust — People believe commitments will be honored and difficult information can be surfaced.
  • Role clarity — Members understand ownership, boundaries, handoffs, and dependencies.
  • Decision authority — The team knows what it can decide and what must be elevated.
  • Operating rhythm — The team has a predictable cadence for coordination, decisions, learning, and adjustment.
  • Constructive dissent — Experts can challenge assumptions without becoming disloyal or defensive.
  • Shared purpose — Different functions can explain the same outcome and why their contribution matters.

blocks.title: ROLE CLARITY
blocks.body: Who owns what?

blocks.title: DECISION RIGHTS
blocks.body: What can this team decide? What must be elevated?

blocks.title: OPERATING RHYTHM
blocks.body: How often do we coordinate, decide, learn, and adjust?

blocks.title: DISSENT + BAD NEWS
blocks.body: How will people surface disagreement, risk, or failure early?
Cross-functional teams exist because no single viewpoint sees the whole system. Trust, clarity, cadence, and psychological safety are operating requirements—not extras.
Choose a hypothetical organizational change. Keep the core truth consistent while changing emphasis, language, and information for five audiences.

blocks.title: commScenario
blocks.body:
• Implement a new workflow
  • Introduce a new technology tool
  • Change a training requirement
  • Redesign a coordination process

blocks.title: EMPLOYEES · impact + support
blocks.body: What is changing? Why? How will people be supported?

blocks.title: SUPERVISORS · expectations + resources
blocks.body: What do supervisors need to do, know, reinforce, or resource?

blocks.title: OTHER FUNCTION · dependencies
blocks.body: What dependencies, handoffs, or coordination matter?

blocks.title: PARTNERS · roles + coordination
blocks.body: What is expected across organizational boundaries?

blocks.title: OVERSIGHT / SENIOR LEADERS · rationale + accountability
blocks.body: What outcome, risk, rationale, and accountability matter?
Strategic communication is disciplined translation. Adapt the emphasis without changing the integrity of the message. Build feedback loops so the message can travel back as well as out.

blocks.title: Accomplish the mission without separating results from character.

blocks.body: Strategic leadership has to hold effectiveness, legality, policy, stewardship, people, risk, accountability, and trust together.
RESULTS WITHOUT TRUST
What happens when a leader achieves the metric but damages credibility, stewardship, or legitimacy?
PROCESS WITHOUT RESULTS
What happens when a leader protects process but cannot create meaningful outcomes?

blocks.title: YOUR LEADERSHIP STANDARD
blocks.body: What principle should remain true even when pressure is high?
Ethical ambition means pursuing meaningful results while staying grounded in principle. Strategic leaders model the behavior the organization must be able to trust.

Strategic leaders still solve problems. The transition is that their highest value increasingly comes from clarity, systems, leader development, alignment, and conditions that keep working when they are not present.

blocks.title: Responsibility often extends beyond formal authority.

blocks.body: LEAD DOWN
Create clarity, resources, trust, development, and accountability.
LEAD UP
Frame issues, surface risk, provide options, and improve senior leaders' understanding.
LEAD ACROSS
Build coalitions, shared understanding, agreements, and reciprocal trust with peers.
LEAD OUT
Coordinate with partners, customers, stakeholders, communities, and external systems.

blocks.title: AN OUTCOME YOU OWN BUT DO NOT FULLY CONTROL
WHAT GIVES YOU CREDIBILITY?
blocks.body: Relationships, evidence, timing, expertise, reliability...

blocks.title: WHAT RELATIONSHIP SHOULD EXIST BEFORE THE CRISIS?

blocks.body: Unity of effort without unity of command is strategic leadership terrain. Authority helps, but alignment also depends on relationships, credibility, timing, evidence, shared purpose, and trust.

blocks.title: Leading a complex system under scrutiny.

blocks.body: During the Deepwater Horizon response, Admiral Thad Allen served as National Incident Commander. The environment included federal agencies, state and local governments, private industry, scientific experts, elected officials, affected communities, media, and the public. No single leader commanded the entire system.

blocks.title: WHO DOES THE LEADER ACTUALLY COMMAND?
WHAT DEFINITIONS OF SUCCESS MAY COMPETE?
WHAT IF OPERATIONS IMPROVE BUT TRUST COLLAPSES?

blocks.body: Strategic leadership is not only command. It is integration: aligning stakeholders with different authorities, information, incentives, risks, and definitions of success.

blocks.title: Where do you need unity of effort without full control?

blocks.body: Think of cross-functional initiatives, technology implementation, workforce development, training, policy, legal coordination, headquarters-field relationships, or partner work.

blocks.title: Strategic failure can look like leadership activity.

blocks.body: Select the two failure modes that create the most risk in your environment.

blocks.title: Two strategic leadership failure risks
blocks.body:
Choose two failure patterns most relevant to your situation.

  • More meetings — More activity without clearer decisions, ownership, or information flow.
  • Vision without means — A direction is announced without resources, accountability, or a credible path.
  • Delegation without intent — Work moves downward but people lack context to make aligned decisions.
  • Communication without feedback — Messages move outward but leaders do not learn what was understood, missed, or resisted.
  • Speed without learning — The organization moves quickly but repeats errors because reflection and adjustment disappear.

blocks.title: COUNTERMEASURE
blocks.body: What practical leader tool or behavior would reduce these risks?

Meetings, taskers, slide decks, and messages are not alignment by themselves. Ask whether decisions are clearer, roles are understood, risk is visible, feedback is flowing, and people know what matters most.

blocks.title: Alignment must be visible before it can be managed.

blocks.body: Use a real or hypothetical initiative. Could every stakeholder state the same intent, priorities, risks, and next learning point?

blocks.title: INTENT · What condition are we creating?
LEARNING RHYTHM · When do we review and adjust?
LEADER ACTIONS
blocks.body: What must leaders reinforce, resource, decide, communicate, or remove?
If different stakeholders carry different assumptions about intent, priorities, risk, or decision timing, alignment is weaker than it appears.

blocks.title: Lead a three-year enterprise modernization effort.

blocks.body: A fictional organization is implementing a major modernization effort affecting people, policy, technology, training, field operations, headquarters, and external partners. Existing mission work must continue. Resources are limited, trust varies, timelines compete, and success depends on adoption—not merely deployment.

blocks.title: 1 · ONE-SENTENCE STRATEGIC INTENT
blocks.body: We are doing ___ so that ___.

blocks.title: 2 · THREE PRIORITIES — NO MORE THAN THREE
3 · STAKEHOLDER MAP
blocks.body: Who approves? Supports? Implements? Must understand? Must be consulted?

blocks.title: 4 · STRATEGIC RISKS
blocks.body: Mission, people, legal/policy, technology, resources, trust...

blocks.title: ASSUMPTION THAT COULD EMBARRASS THE STRATEGY

blocks.body: The job is not to create a technical implementation plan. The job is to create strategic alignment: clear intent, disciplined priorities, visible stakeholders and risk, and leader behavior that supports adoption.

blocks.title: Brief the thinking—not just the recommendation.

blocks.body: Your brief should make the desired condition, the things that must hold, the strategic risks, and the decision needed immediately visible.

blocks.title: INTENT · desired condition + why it matters
PRIORITIES · the three things that must hold
RISKS · what could fail + how we will learn
DECISION NEEDED · what do you need from leadership now?

blocks.body: If the brief becomes too tactical, ask: What strategic condition are we trying to create? If it becomes too abstract, ask: What decision or leader action is required now?
